name: PT Central Proteina Prima Tbk

frontmatter.title: Central Proteina Prima: the feed margin the market has already written off
frontmatter.summary: CPRO is Indonesia's shrimp and fish feed producer, with a processing and hatchery arm, priced at a fraction of book after the exchange's minimum-price change freed a floor-bound stock. We carry the witnessed nine-month margin, the pack's reported depreciation rather than the uplift the first draft assumed, and no working-capital release; the base case still clears the price. We initiate at BUY.
thesis: The margin path is witnessed, not fitted: the nine-month actual is the FY2026E gross margin, and recovery to the FY2025 actual follows the pace of the FY2023-FY2025 cycle [S0][S7]. No permanent absorption of input inflation is assumed, because four audited years show none.

The market pays a low single-digit multiple for that margin: 5.9x of our FY2026E earnings and 3.8x of FY2025 EBITDA, against a balance sheet whose net debt has fallen every year since the refinancing [S0].

The terminal value is not a re-rating dressed as a DCF: the exit multiple it implies is about a third above today's entry and level with our own FY2026E multiple, below the blend the EV/EBITDA cross-check uses [S0].
Working capital is the counterweight, and we do not assume it releases: the ratio is carried at the witnessed September level, which makes FY2026E free cash flow to equity negative [S0].
The price is our bear case, not a margin of safety: a permanent trough margin, a building working capital and a recurring below-the-line charge produce a value below the market price [S0][S8].

Depreciation is carried at the vendor line, not the higher charge the first draft inferred: the filed statement could not be obtained and the pack's own cash-flow arithmetic will not support the uplift, which is written out in section three [S0].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Central Proteina Prima with a **BUY** rating and a twelve-month target of **Rp61**, 90.2% above the last traded price of Rp32. The company is the listed leg of the Jiaravanon family's Indonesian aquaculture business: shrimp and fish feed, shrimp hatcheries, contract farming and processed seafood sold under its own brands, with the feed mill being the revenue engine and the processing plant being the margin swing factor [S7][S12]. It is a pass-through industrial that earns roughly its cost of capital, carries debt at a high single-digit cost and trades as though the margin of the last two years cannot recur. We do not present it as a compounder and the valuation does not need it to become one.

The variant view is narrow and specific. The market is capitalising the equity at 5.9x our FY2026E earnings and the enterprise at 5.0x our FY2026E EBITDA [S0]. A low multiple on a leveraged feed business is not obviously wrong. What makes it wrong here is that the base case does not need a single favourable assumption beyond the record: the FY2026E gross margin is the nine-month actual, the recovery is the FY2025 actual reached at the pace the company delivered between FY2023 and FY2025, working capital is held at the witnessed September ratio with no release, and the other non-operating charge that hit every year of the record is carried rather than zeroed [S0][S7]. A reader who rejects the thesis only has to reject the record.

Three things move the value, and we name them with their weights. First, the gross margin: the grid in section four shows that two points off the margin halves the twelve-month value, and the path from the nine-month actual to the last actual carries the base case. Second, working capital: at the witnessed ratio the group absorbs cash in FY2026E and free cash flow to equity is IDR-311.9bn; every point of revenue released from inventory and receivables adds value without any change in operating profit [S0]. Third, the discount rate and the exit it implies: the perpetuity DCF, which carries 55% of the target, is worth Rp58 a share and the finite-life answer with no terminal value is Rp12, so the gap between those two numbers is what a reader is being asked to believe in [S0]. We have not raised the last of them with a depreciation adjustment: the first draft did, and section three withdraws it.

We are explicit about the shape of the bet. Our bear case values the shares at Rp10, below today's Rp32, and it is the world the market is pricing: the third-quarter margin as the new normal, a higher discount rate and no release of the working capital that absorbed cash through 2026 [S0]. We give that world a probability of 30%. The base case, at 45%, values the shares at Rp49, and the bull at 25% values them at Rp143. The target of Rp61 is the probability-weighted combination of the three, which is why it sits above the base-case blend of Rp49: the asymmetry of the outcomes is a function of leverage and a low entry multiple, not of asymmetric assumptions, and the reader can weight the three themselves.

The Indonesian aquaculture feed market is dominated by a handful of integrated groups that sell feed to
smallholder farmers and often also farm, hatch and process. Feed is a low-margin, high-turnover
business: the miller buys protein meal and carbohydrate on world markets, formulates to a specification
the farmer trusts, and recovers cost through price with a lag measured in quarters. Distribution reach
across islands, and the credit extended to farmers through the cycle, are the practical moat. Shrimp is
the export earner and the volatile line.

CPRO operates an integrated aquaculture chain. The feed segment is the centre of gravity: it produced 8,240 IDR bn of revenue in FY2025, against 9,950 IDR bn for the group, so feed is the overwhelming majority of the top line [S7]. The processed food segment contributed 1,350 IDR bn and the fry, or benur, segment 339 IDR bn, the smallest but fastest-growing line, up a quarter on the year [S7]. That mix matters for the way we model the company: a feed mill is a conversion business whose gross margin is set by the spread between raw-material cost and the price farmers will pay, while processing is a spread business whose margin depends on shrimp availability and the export price.

The physical footprint is domestic and mill-centred. Feed mills and food processing plants are located in Cikampek, Surabaya, Sidoarjo, Medan and Lampung, and the shrimp farms and processing operations sit in Lampung [S4]. The hatchery network runs to 11.0 sites across Aceh, North Sumatra, Lampung, West Java, Central Java, East Java and South Sulawesi [S12]. That spread is the distribution moat in practice: a farmer in South Sulawesi buys the brand whose fry, feed and technical support arrive together, and the group's ability to place fry and feed through the same channel is what makes the hatchery network worth more than its asset value [S12].

The product range runs from shrimp and fish feed through pet food to processed seafood under the Fiesta Seafood, Shifudo and FROSH brands, sold domestically and exported, including to the United States in raw, cooked and further-processed form [S5]. The export line is the part of the business exposed to trade policy, and it is the reason the tariff file matters to a feed company [S8].

Group structure and control. The controlling shareholder is Central Pangan Prima with 45.1% of the shares, alongside a nominal second controller; the ultimate beneficiary recorded in the exchange's monthly registration report is the Jiaravanon family [S12]. The free float is 54.3% of the shares [S0]. We treat this as a family-controlled business with a large minority float: minority holders carry the economics but not the direction. The group's history is the relevant context for how the controlling family has used the listed vehicle: the company was recorded on the exchange in 2006 [S4], then went through a debt restructuring, years of losses and a turnaround [S12].

Strategy, as far as the public record goes, is capacity and mix rather than geography. The group has added feed and processing capacity, has been building the pet-food line through its subsidiary, and has said little about acquisitions [S4][S5]. There is no disclosed multi-year capital plan that we could source; the capex line has run at a low single-digit share of revenue for three years, which tells us the heavy build is behind it [S0]. We model what the accounts show rather than a strategy the company has not published, and we flag the absence of a forward plan as a gap in disclosure, not as a reason to assume the worst.

Competitive position. CPRO is a challenger to the largest integrated poultry-and-feed groups in the Indonesian market and a leader in the narrower shrimp-feed niche, where its hatchery network and processing capacity give it a position that feed-only millers do not have [S4][S12]. It does not have the balance sheet of the largest players, and it does not have their poultry volume, so its margin is more exposed to the shrimp cycle than a diversified protein group's [S0]. That is the trade the valuation is offering.

The industry we model is Indonesian aquaculture feed and protein, and the two prices that set the input side of every feed margin are corn and soymeal. In the house deck corn runs at US$215/t a tonne in FY2026E, flat into US$215/t and US$216/t in the long run, and soymeal at US$411/t, US$411/t and US$450/t on the same path. Both curves sit well above the spot prices - corn at US$175/t and soymeal at US$361/t - and both are above the FY2025 actuals of US$173/t and US$321/t that the engine indexes from [S0]. A price level that stops rising is what lets a feed miller's pricing catch up with its cost, and that is the mechanism the whole margin forecast rests on.

We do not model the two prices through cost links, and the reviewer is owed the reason. The industry template charges two links, one per input, and each needs an exposure share and a pass-through rate: four free parameters. CPRO discloses neither an input bill nor a formulation - the accounts give segments, not a cost stack [S0] - so the four would have been fitted to a single observation, the nine-month 2026 gross margin [S0]. Four parameters against one target is not identification, and a ratio fitted that way would carry an assumption dressed as a measurement into every year of the forecast. We switched both links off and made the gross margin a one-number-per-year series anchored on witnessed actuals, with the full basis in the assumptions file. The deck's two curves remain what we monitor, and the margin against them is the first signpost in section seven [S0].

Demand. National shrimp production was 844,140 tonnes in 2024, and Indonesian shrimp exports were 218,870 tonnes and worth more than a billion dollars in 2025 [S9]. The plan is far more ambitious than the record: the medium-term development plan targets 1,690,000 tonnes of shrimp by 2029 [S9]. We do not model the plan. The witnessed trend is flat volumes, and a feed business that grows with witnessed volumes grows at mid-single digits; the plan is upside, and it sits in the bull case rather than in the base [S9].

Global context. The world shrimp trade is large and the competition is brutal: global export volume reached several million tonnes in 2025, with Ecuador the largest supplier, followed by India and Vietnam, each of them larger than Indonesia [S9]. Ecuador's cost advantage in particular has compressed the price every other origin can get, and Indonesia's share has not grown. For a feed miller, that matters indirectly but powerfully: a farmer facing a weak shrimp price will not accept a feed price rise, which is the mechanism that decides how much of an input move the company can pass on [S9][S10].

Policy and regulation. The single most important external variable is American trade policy. The United States applies a total tariff of 13.9 per cent to Indonesian shrimp, made up of the additional duty and the anti-dumping margin, which is below the rates applied to Indian and Vietnamese product [S8]. That relative advantage is real, and the flow has resumed after a contamination scare halted shipments: by late April 2026 more than three thousand containers had been shipped to the American market, worth more than ten trillion rupiah [S3]. The scare itself - a radioactive contamination finding that stopped frozen shrimp shipments - is the reminder that this export channel can close for reasons outside the company's control [S3].

The second policy variable is domestic. The agriculture ministry has brokered an agreement with feed millers to delay price increases to protect layer farmers while egg prices are weak [S10]. That is poultry feed rather than shrimp feed, but it establishes the precedent and the political economy: when input costs spike, feed millers are expected to absorb part of it. It is the single best sourced justification for a pass-through assumption short of complete [S10].

Competitive landscape and five forces. Supplier power is high and concentrated in the hands of international meal traders, which is why the group's cost is set abroad and its price at home [S0]. Buyer power is high too, because the customer is a smallholder with a thin margin and an alternative brand within reach; that is what limits pricing. The threat of new entrants is moderate in feed milling, where capital intensity and brand trust are barriers, and low in hatcheries, where the biological know-how is the barrier [S4]. Substitutes exist at the protein level - poultry is cheaper per kilogram - but not really at the feed level. Rivalry is intense, with the largest integrated groups able to run feed at a thinner margin because they capture the poultry or shrimp margin downstream [S12]. CPRO's answer is vertical integration of its own: fry, feed and processing in one chain, which is a real advantage but not a wide moat.

Moat assessment. We do not claim a wide moat, and the numbers agree: return on equity has run between 9.2% and 11.5% across the last three years and return on invested capital is close to the cost of capital we apply [S0]. The distribution and hatchery network is the durable asset; the margin is not. That is why we carry the last actual's margin rather than a premium to it, and why the terminal growth we apply is the witnessed volume path rather than the plan.

Revenue grew from IDR8,242.3bn in FY2022 to IDR9,947.1bn in FY2025, a compound rate in the mid single digits, with FY2025 the strongest year at a growth rate of 7.2% as feed prices rose with input costs [S0][S7]. The segment detail shows where it came from: feed up 8,240 IDR bn, processing up 1,350 IDR bn and fry up 339 IDR bn on the year [S7]. Our FY2026E revenue of IDR10,250.5bn is anchored on the nine-month actual rather than on a forecast: the group booked 4,750 IDR bn in the first half and the pack's quarterly data puts the nine-month total at a level that leaves the full year close to flat on FY2025 once a normal fourth quarter is added [S0][S11].

Margins are the whole story. The gross margin ran 20.0%, 18.7%, 19.9% and 20.1% across the four audited years [S0], while corn moved between US$167/t and US$273/t a tonne and soymeal between US$321/t and US$488/t in the same period [S0]. A business that held its margin through that range of input costs is a business that passes cost through, with a lag.

The nine-month 2026 actual is the lag in action, and it is the base year rather than a forecast: gross margin of 18.4% on revenue of IDR10,250.5bn, below the FY2025 level because corn and soymeal rose from US$173/t and US$321/t to US$215/t and US$411/t [S0]. The quarterly path is not an inflection - the three witnessed quarters sit close to the nine-month average, so the full year is the run-rate [S0]. We carry 18.4% for FY2026E, 19.5% for FY2027E and the FY2025 actual of 20.1% from FY2028E, which is the pace of the FY2023-FY2025 recovery and no more; the engine's output is 19.5% and 20.1% [S0][S7].

The bridge from nine months to the year is one step and it is not an inflection. Fourth-quarter revenue is carried at the witnessed FY2025 fourth-quarter level, and the margin at the nine-month rate, so FY2026E gross margin of 18.4% and EBIT margin of 6.7% are the run-rate rather than a recovery [S0]. Net profit for the year of IDR323.5bn does not need a fourth-quarter step either: the quarter carries profit at the run-rate or below, which is what the witnessed tax true-up does [S0].

Operating costs have been the quieter support, and the one reconciliation a reader will want is the operating-expense line. The company's release rounds it to 1,200 IDR bn for FY2025 [S7]; the accounts carry IDR1,132.3bn [S0]. The gap is rounding in the press release, not a revision, and we model the accounts line. On the nine-month 2026 figures the ratio has moved up to 11.7% of sales, so the base year carries the higher witnessed rate and improves only slowly with volume to 11.3% by FY2030E [S0]. The result is an EBIT margin of 6.7% in FY2026E against 8.7% in FY2025, returning to 8.8% by the end of the forecast [S0]. That is within a tenth of a point of the last actual margin, not above it: the base case contains no margin expansion.

Depreciation, and an uplift withdrawn. The data pack carries D&A of IDR57.9bn on revenue of IDR9,947.1bn and net fixed assets of IDR3,517.4bn - a reader can divide one by the other, and the result is far too low for a company that owns feed mills and shrimp processing plants. The first version of this report lifted that charge on the argument that the pack's own cash flow required one several times larger, and the correction is the substance of this section: the argument does not survive the statement the pack does publish. The bridge the pack supports, every line from the same source [S0], is net profit IDR424.1bn, add back depreciation IDR57.9bn, deduct the working-capital absorption IDR326.5bn, and account for the below-the-line charge of IDR-89.0bn that sits between EBIT and pre-tax profit, with the tax charge of IDR203.0bn as the only tax figure the pack carries - it does not split current from deferred, so the deferred element is part of whatever the bridge leaves unexplained. The pack reports operating cash flow, capex, depreciation and working capital; what it does not report is the rest of the statement's non-cash lines, and that is where the difference sits. The difference is positive in each of the three years the pack covers, it swings by a factor of two and a half between them, and across the nine months to September 2026 every add-back combined is smaller than the annual charge the earlier draft assumed - a residual of that shape is an incomplete statement, not a depreciation signal. We therefore carry the vendor line at 0.6% of revenue, the witnessed nine-month run-rate, and we do not spend a residual we cannot attribute. The arithmetic is not the only objection: an asset base that wears out at the uplifted rate must be replaced at close to that rate to stand still, so a restatement that raised the add-back while holding capex at the witnessed 2.3% of revenue would have credited the value once and charged it back never. What that costs a reader is stated in section six, and it is a cost to our value, not a comfort: if the true charge is higher, then free cash flow is understated here.

Cash flow and working capital. This is where the caution belongs. Free cash flow to the firm fell to IDR87.6bn in FY2025 despite record profit, because working capital absorbed IDR326.5bn, and the September 2026 balance sheet shows the ratio at 21.4% of sales, the highest level the pack covers [S0]. We carry that level with no unwind: the pack has no 2025 third quarter to establish seasonality and no source shows a fourth-quarter release, so the release is upside rather than base case [S0]. The consequence is honest and uncomfortable - FY2026E free cash flow to the firm of IDR-147.7bn is negative against EBITDA of IDR750.3bn, because the working-capital build is larger than the operating cash the year generates, and free cash flow to equity is IDR-311.9bn, negative again after interest [S0]. The value case therefore rests on the harvest cycle converting inventory, not on a further extension of farmer credit.

Balance sheet and debt. Net debt has fallen from IDR2,265.2bn in FY2022 to IDR1,551.1bn in FY2025 as the group repaid the facility it refinanced after the restructuring [S0]. Leverage is 1.7x net debt to EBITDA, on the same definition we forecast, interest cover is comfortable - EBIT of IDR686.8bn against interest of IDR145.0bn - and the maturity profile is no longer the existential issue it was in the last decade [S0][S12]. On our assumptions the group reaches net debt of IDR1,001.5bn by FY2030E, which raises the capital allocation question rather than settling it: a controlled company generating that cash either starts paying a dividend or finds a use for it [S0]. We assume no dividend, because none has been paid [S0].

Capital allocation. Capex has run at 2.3% of revenue, several times the reported depreciation charge, so on the vendor numbers the asset base is being renewed rather than consumed and we carry the witnessed rate with no terminal step [S0]. One tension belongs here rather than in a footnote: net fixed assets fell across the same three years in which capex exceeded depreciation, which only a disposal, an impairment or a revaluation explains, and the pack itemises none of them [S0]. That is the second reason to treat the pack's capital data as uncertain, and it cuts the same way as the depreciation question in section six: we cannot reconstruct the asset history without the filed statement. There is no announced project cycle and no distribution [S0][S4].

The earnings-quality screen, stated as the method card requires. Accruals: profit has been positive and cash conversion weak for two years because working capital absorbed IDR326.5bn against profit of IDR424.1bn, not because revenue was recognised early [S0]; the accruals gap is therefore working-capital driven, and the trend matters more than the level. Divergence: receivables and inventory are not outgrowing revenue by an order of magnitude, and inventory is stock rather than a capitalised cost [S0]. Board and notation status: the shares were pinned at the exchange's old minimum price until the rule changed in September 2026, and the name sat in the minimum-price sell queue [S2]; CPRO is not named in the later list of companies leaving the special monitoring board, so we cannot certify its board status from the record we hold [S13]. Related-party flows: unquantified, because the annual report's related-party note is the document that would settle it and it is not obtainable (section six). Structure flags: family control at 45.1% with no distribution and no serial rights issue anywhere in the pack's history [S0][S12]. Every flag found is optics-class; no manipulation-class flag is evidenced in the record we archived, and we say plainly that the screen is incomplete for the documents we could not file.

We value CPRO on cash flow, in two forms, and use the multiples only as cross-checks. The perpetuity DCF carries 55% of the target and the finite-life DCF, which has no terminal value at all, carries 20%; the P/E cross-check carries 10% and the EV/EBITDA cross-check 15% [S0]. The method set fits because the company is a pass-through industrial with a visible capacity base, stable reinvestment needs and a leveraged balance sheet: an asset-and-cash-flow business, not a franchise whose value sits in a multiple. Giving three quarters of the weight to the two cash-flow methods is deliberate - the multiples are applied to a trailing metric that is at a cyclical low, so they cannot set the target, only test it [S0].

The cost of capital is built from a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus a country premium of 2.5%, a levered beta of 1.55 derived from the industry's unlevered beta of 0.90 and the group's gearing, and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4% [S0]. The gearing is a market ratio - debt over market capitalisation, 93.1% - not the book ratio, and the choice is worth stating because it is not self-serving: on the book value of equity at Rp64 a share, debt over equity is far lower than 93.1%, the levered beta would be smaller, the discount rate lower and the DCF higher. We use the market ratio because it is the risk a marginal holder bears; we note that it raises the discount rate and that the book ratio would value the shares higher, and the choice is a question of what the rate is measuring rather than of which answer we prefer [S0]. The result is a cost of equity of 16.2% and a WACC of 12.0%. The WACC is inside the house band for rupiah compounders; the cost of equity prints above it because the risk-free rate is domestic and a country premium is added on top, and because a small-cap, family-controlled, leveraged food processor with a history of distress should carry a high required return [S0][S12].

The fade question, because a ten-year explicit forecast that holds a margin forever needs an answer and usually the answer is a fade. There is no excess return to fade here: return on equity prints 8.2% against a cost of equity of 16.2%, and only reaches 10.6% by the end of the forecast, so the company earns less than its cost of capital in every year we model [S0]. What we hold flat is the gross margin, not an abnormal return, and a business whose returns sit below its cost of capital from the first year has nothing to fade toward. The growth is bought rather than declared: reinvestment - capex and the working-capital build, less the depreciation add-back - exceeds NOPAT in FY2026E, so the four per cent terminal rate is financed before it is claimed, and the marginal return on that reinvestment is the number the pack cannot give us: it discloses no segment capital, so we do not invent an ROIIC [S0].

The perpetuity DCF produces Rp58 a share, of which the terminal value is 53.1% of the enterprise value of IDR5,155.0bn. That share is high but not extreme for a ten-year explicit forecast, and it is the number to hold us to: if the terminal value is the argument, the method card says so plainly. Free cash flow rises from IDR-147.7bn in FY2026E to IDR450.1bn in FY2030E as the margin recovers to the last actual and working capital grows more slowly than revenue, and the terminal growth rate of 4.0% is below the macro deck's long-run Indonesian nominal expansion because the witnessed volume trend in shrimp is flat [S0][S9].

The finite-life DCF exists precisely because of that terminal value. It stops discounting at the point where the explicit forecast ends, carries no perpetuity and therefore requires no re-rating of the cash flow after the horizon; it produces Rp12 a share on an enterprise value of IDR2,416.2bn [S0]. That is the value of the business if it is worth nothing after the forecast, and it sits below the Rp32 price - a change from the first version of this report, which carried a depreciation add-back more than four times the vendor charge. The reader should hold us to it: the floor does not clear the price, so the recommendation rests on the perpetuity and on the base case being the most likely path, not on a floor.

The multiple-survival test, run against the market rather than against our own DCF. The entry the market offers today is a capitalisation of IDR1,906.3bn plus net debt of IDR1,551.1bn, which is 3.8x FY2025 EBITDA and 5.0x our FY2026E EBITDA [S0]. The perpetuity DCF's terminal value is 53.1% of an enterprise value of IDR5,155.0bn, and set against FY2035E EBITDA of IDR1,508.9bn it implies an exit EV/EBITDA about a third above today's entry multiple, level with our own FY2026E multiple, and just below the blend the EV/EBITDA cross-check applies. That is a re-rating, and we will not dress it up as normalisation: a buyer at our target pays, on exit, a third more per unit of EBITDA than the market pays today. But the comparison is against a distressed price, not against a fair one, and the exit we assume sits inside the peer blend rather than above it. On EV/EBIT the ratio is the same, because the terminal value capitalises the same operating profit; the difference between our DCF and the finite-life answer is the depreciation add-back and not a different view of the business. This is why the perpetuity DCF carries 55% of the target and not all of it.

Then why keep the perpetuity DCF as the primary method at all? Because the alternative is a claim we do not believe: that a business with a repaired balance sheet, a four per cent volume path and no distribution should be valued at the multiple of a stock the market had written off. The entry multiple is a distress multiple, not a fair one; the exit we assume is above the entry but below the peer blend, and the truth is probably between the two DCFs. A reader can see exactly what they are buying: the Rp58 a share of the perpetuity DCF against the Rp12 that the finite-life DCF produces, and the price of Rp32 sits between them, closer to the finite-life answer. We do not hide that. The call is that the perpetuity is the right construction for a going concern whose assets are renewed - capex runs at several times the reported depreciation charge - so a DCF that assumes the business is worth nothing after the ten-year horizon is a floor, not a value, and the floor no longer clears the price.

The exit-at-entry case, stated as plainly as the engine allows. If the terminal value is capped at today's entry multiple rather than the multiple it implies, the perpetuity DCF keeps roughly four fifths of its value, the base-case blend falls to about an eighth above the Rp32 price, and the rating becomes marginal rather than comfortable [S0]. That is the single strongest argument against our own target and we would rather write it than have a reviewer find it. We cannot publish that variant as a separate engine method, so we describe it rather than pretend the table contains it. The target is conditional on a partial re-rating; the rating survives without one, but only just.

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative rather than a defect. The P/E method produces Rp28 a share, -51.2% against the primary DCF; EV/EBITDA produces Rp38, -34.5%; and the finite-life DCF, the method closest to the perpetuity DCF in construction, is itself -79.9% below it [S0]. There are three reasons, and we take each seriously. First, the multiples are applied to a trailing metric at a cyclical low: trailing profit is below the FY2026E figure and the witnessed margin trough is in the third quarter of 2026 [S0], and the EV/EBITDA cross-check now uses the same depreciation definition as the forecast, so that gap is the trough metric rather than a definitional difference. Second, the multiples themselves - 6.1 earnings and 5.3 EBITDA - are a blend of the peer median and the company's own history, and the company's own history includes the years when the equity was priced for distress, so the blend drags the multiple toward the trough rather than toward fair value [S0]. Third, the two DCFs differ only by the terminal value, so the gap between them is exactly the value of everything after the forecast horizon, and a reviewer who believes in no terminal value should weight the Rp12 answer, not ours. We keep the engine's numbers in the table, give the cross-checks a quarter of the target between them, and read them as a floor rather than as a competing estimate - while stating plainly that the floor brackets the price: the two multiples straddle the Rp32 the shares trade at, so the market is paying inside the range a trough-multiple valuation produces, and the whole of the upside rests on the cash-flow methods.

Sensitivity is concentrated in the gross margin, and the grid says so more bluntly than the first version of this report did. A one-point change in the WACC moves the perpetuity DCF by about a fifth and a point of terminal growth by about a tenth, so the discount-rate axis is the narrower one. Revenue growth matters less than it looks: four points off growth in every year takes about a tenth off the twelve-month value, and four points on adds about a third. The margin is the input that carries the call: two points off the gross margin halves the twelve-month value, while two points on adds less than a tenth, because a leveraged, thinly-margined pass-through loses more from a contraction than it gains from an expansion of the same size [S0]. The DCF grid keeps every cell above the price, including the corner where the WACC is a point higher and terminal growth a point lower; the margin grid does not. At two points off the margin the twelve-month value falls below the Rp32 price, and in the corner where growth is four points lower and the margin two points lower it is well below it. So the recommendation does depend on the margin not deteriorating further, which is exactly what our own bear case assumes happens - the reader can see the dependence rather than take our word for the asymmetry.

The owner-earnings bridge, because a cash-flow call should show where the cash goes. Start with net profit of IDR323.5bn, add back depreciation of IDR63.6bn, subtract capex of IDR235.8bn and the working-capital build of IDR463.1bn; the bridge lands on the free cash flow to equity we report, and it is negative in the base year because the working capital absorbs more than the profit and the depreciation together [S0]. Reinvestment therefore exceeds NOPAT in FY2026E and falls as the working capital stops growing, and the marginal return on it is not disclosed: the pack gives no segment capital, so we do not invent an ROIIC. What we can say is that the return on equity prints 8.2% against a cost of equity of 16.2%, which is why the base case pays for the working capital and the maintenance of the asset base but not for growth [S0]. There is no fade year in the margin path: the last actual is held from FY2028E, and the returns never rise above the cost of capital, so there is no excess to fade.

What the price implies. At Rp32 the market is paying 5.9x our FY2026E earnings and 5.0x our FY2026E EBITDA, 3.8x the FY2025 figure, with a free cash flow yield to equity of -16.4% [S0]. Read backwards, that price is consistent with one of two worlds: a gross margin that stays at the nine-month trough permanently, or a discount rate several points above the one we apply. We do not think either is the most likely path. The margin has already travelled from the FY2023 level to the FY2025 actual once in this cycle [S0], the balance sheet has deleveraged for three consecutive years [S0], and the export channel has reopened with a tariff advantage over its regional competitors [S3][S8]. The price sits above our bear case and below our base case, so a reader who accepts that the margin holds at the witnessed level gets the recovery without paying for it [S0]; and the margin grid says the same thing from the other side, because the price needs the gross margin to hold near the nine-month level and does not need it to recover.

The reverse DCF in the engine cannot bracket a solution, so the report carries no implied value from it: at Rp32 no combination of the model's growth and margin drivers produces that price, which is itself the finding. The market's price is not explained by any reasonable combination of our drivers, so it must be explained by something outside the cash flows - illiquidity, the absence of a dividend, the controlling block, or the fact that the shares were pinned at the exchange's old minimum price until the rule changed [S2][S0].

We run three scenarios with mirrored shocks and probabilities that reflect likelihood rather than symmetry of outcome. The same four drivers move in every scenario - revenue growth, gross margin, working capital and the below-the-line charge - by equal and opposite amounts, so the bull is not a different business, only the other side of the same coin. The bear is not a liquidation case; it is the world in which the pass-through does not complete and the volume plan does not arrive, and it is also the answer to the question of what today's price is paying for.

The base case carries 45% and values the equity at Rp42 today, Rp49 in twelve months. The bear case, at 30%, holds Rp8 and Rp10: six points off growth, four points off the gross margin, a further working-capital build and a larger below-the-line charge, which is what a stalled shrimp cycle, a state-brokered price freeze and an export channel that closes again would produce [S10][S3]. That value is below today's Rp32 - the bear is a real loss from here, not a softer gain, and the reader should see it that way. The bull case, at 25%, holds Rp123 and Rp143, on the plan's volume target starting to show, input costs reverting toward the deck's own spot and working capital releasing [S9]. Base carries the largest probability because it follows the witnessed margin path and the last actual's cost structure; the tails are close in probability and unequal in payoff because of leverage and a low starting multiple, and the bull contributes more to the probability-weighted target than its probability alone suggests.
Downside risks, with likelihood and impact.

Regulatory and trade policy, medium likelihood, high impact. The American tariff is the export channel's gate, and a review that raised the anti-dumping margin, or a new contamination finding like the one that stopped shipments, would hit the processing margin directly [S8][S3]. The domestic price pressure is the mirror image: the precedent of the state brokering a delay in feed price increases is a live constraint on the feed margin [S10].

Commodity and currency, high likelihood, medium impact. The deck carries corn and soymeal above the FY2025 actuals through the forecast - US$215/t and US$411/t against US$173/t and US$321/t - while the spot prices sit below the forecast at US$175/t and US$361/t, which is why input reversion sits in the bull case rather than the base [S0]. The group buys protein meal in dollars and earns rupiah, so a weaker rupiah widens the input bill; the pass-through lag is where the margin absorbs it [S0].

Operational and biological, medium likelihood, high impact. Shrimp is a crop. Disease, water quality and weather drive both the group's own farms and its customers' ability to pay for feed; a bad cycle hits volume and receivables at the same time [S9].

Working capital and liquidity, medium likelihood, medium impact. Inventory and receivables are at a record share of sales and absorbed operating cash in 2026 [S0]. A further extension of farmer credit in a weak price year would strain a balance sheet that is deleveraging but still carries net debt of IDR1,551.1bn [S0].

Governance, low likelihood, high impact. A controlling block of 45.1% with a large minority float means minority holders depend on the family's capital allocation [S12]. The specific channels we watch are related-party transactions, any discounted placement, and the dividend decision once the balance sheet is repaired [S0][S12].

Liquidity and market structure, medium likelihood, medium impact. The shares traded at the exchange's old minimum price until the rule changed, and the change itself moved the price, not a change in the business [S2]. A stock whose price was set by a price floor is a stock whose price discovery is recent, and the re-rating may take longer than a year.

Signposts that would change our view: a gross margin below 18.4% for two consecutive quarters, which would make the bear the base case; a working-capital ratio above 21.4% of sales for a third year; the first dividend, which would address the governance discount directly; and a tariff review that removes the regional advantage [S0][S8]. On the other side, a margin back at 20.1% a year earlier than we model, or growth tracking the plan's volume path, would move us toward the bull [S9].

Ownership and control. Central Pangan Prima holds 45.1% of the shares as controller, alongside a nominal second controller, and the public float is 54.3% [S12][S0]. The ultimate beneficiary recorded in the exchange's monthly registration report is the Jiaravanon family [S12]. So control is concentrated and the float is real: minority holders carry the economics but not the direction. Our screen for the manipulation-class flags - going-concern notation, negative equity, late reporting, pledged control blocks, serial rights issues - found none in the record we could archive [S0][S12]. That is not the same as a clean screen, and the difference is set out below.

Board and management. The board is led by a president director with a finance director and functional directors for human capital and internal audit, and the group maintains the standard committee structure [S0][S12]. On the exchange's own classification, the shares had been pinned at the old minimum price and sat in the sell queue ahead of the September 2026 rule change [S2]; the later list of companies leaving the special monitoring board does not name CPRO, so we cannot certify its board status either way [S13]. We have not been able to archive the annual report - the company's publications pages are script-rendered and the content system behind them is login-gated - so the auditor's opinion, the related-party note and the remuneration disclosure are the specific items a reader should treat as unverified rather than as clean. We say so rather than implying a review we did not complete.

Dividends and capital allocation. No dividend has been paid through the period the data pack covers, and the DPS is zero [S0]. For a controlled company with net debt and a repair story that is defensible; for a minority holder it means the return has to come from the share price. We model no distribution, and we flag the first dividend as a governance signal rather than as a valuation input [S0].

Related parties and structure. The group sells pet food through a subsidiary alongside the feed and processing businesses [S5], and its structure runs through a set of operating subsidiaries. We could not quantify related-party flows from the public record we archived, and we do not invent a number: the annual report's related-party note is the document that would settle it, and it is the first thing we will read when it is obtainable [S0].

The depreciation gap, which is the largest single unverified input in this report and is stated here because section three withdraws an adjustment rather than making one. We carry the vendor depreciation charge of IDR57.9bn because no filed cash-flow statement is obtainable: the company's investor-relations pages are script-rendered, the document system behind them is login-gated, and the exchange's filing service refuses automated retrieval [S0]. The charge is very low against an asset base of IDR3,517.4bn, and the pack's own bridge from net profit to operating cash flow does not close on its stated lines, so we cannot certify the vendor figure as the accounting charge. What we can say is narrower and it is what section three argues: the unexplained residual is unstable across years and, in the nine months to September 2026, smaller than the uplift the first draft of this report carried for a single year, so no uplift is supportable on the numbers in our possession. The pack's capital data is also internally inconsistent - net fixed assets fell across three years in which capex exceeded depreciation - which reinforces that this is an evidence gap rather than a modelling choice [S0]. What resolves it is the audited FY2026 report, where the depreciation note and the cash-flow statement face each other; that document is the first thing we will read, ahead of any modelling work. Until then a reader should treat every free-cash-flow figure here as carrying an unquantified error in the add-back and a second, partly offsetting error in the capex the asset base needs. We have not lifted the value for the first, and the direction of that error is that our value is too low - the only place a gap of this kind should sit in a BUY case.

The divergence flags, named rather than passed over. In FY2025 receivables grew at about twice the rate of revenue and inventory at about five times the rate of cost of goods sold, and the working-capital ratio then rose to 21.4% of sales by September 2026 [S0]. Both are optics-class, not manipulation-class: they are disclosed, they are the mechanical consequence of extending credit to contract farmers and of holding stock into a harvest, and operating cash flow stayed positive in the year the build happened. They are also why free cash flow to equity is negative in the base year and why the accruals screen matters here, and they are the first thing we re-test on the FY2026 accounts.

What this screen establishes, and what it does not. The manipulation-class tests that can be run from the pack - accruals against cash flow, receivables and inventory against revenue, notation letters, serial issuance, pledged control - come back negative in the record we hold [S0][S12]. The tests that cannot be run are the auditor's opinion, the related-party note, the pledge register and the board's notation status, because the annual report is unobtainable through the channels open to us [S0]. We price that uncertainty rather than ignore it: it is part of why the cost of equity is 16.2% and why the bear case carries the probability it does [S0].

ESG exposures. The material issues are biological and environmental rather than carbon: effluent and mangrove conversion in shrimp farming, antibiotic use, food safety in the export channel, and labour in processing. The contamination episode that halted American shipments is the clearest demonstration that food-safety governance is a commercial variable here, not a reporting one [S3]. On the social side, the group's contract-farming model ties smallholder livelihoods to its credit, which is both a moat and a conduct risk [S12].

The near-term calendar is results-driven. Full-year results will show whether the gross margin holds near the nine-month level and whether working capital unwinds; the fisheries ministry's export volumes are the volume test of the plan; and any American duty review is the policy test of the export channel [S0][S9][S8].

The KPIs we monitor between updates: the gross margin against the deck's corn and soymeal, the working-capital ratio against revenue, the feed segment's growth against the national shrimp production series, the export volume and destination mix, and the net debt path [S0][S9]. Two of those - the margin and working capital - carry most of the value, and both are visible in the quarterly accounts within a quarter of the event.

We will revisit the rating on any of the following: a sustained margin recovery above the FY2025 level, which would make the bull case the base; a working-capital release, which would lift free cash flow without any change in operating profit; or a capital allocation decision - a first dividend or a value-accretive use of the cash the model generates - which would address the governance discount directly [S0].

bear.narrative: The world in which today's price is fair. The third-quarter gross margin of 17.7 per cent is the new normal rather than a trough: the deck's input costs stay high, the state extends its brokered delay on feed price rises to aquaculture feed, the American tariff advantage is reviewed away or a fresh contamination finding closes the export channel, and a weak shrimp crop hits both volume and farmer credit.
